About the California Environmental Protection Agency

In 1991, California’s environmental authority was unified in a single Cabinet level agency—the California Environmental Protection Agency (CalEPA). Our mission is to restore, protect and enhance the environment, to ensure public health, environmental quality and economic vitality. We fulfill our mission by developing, implementing and enforcing environmental laws that regulate air, water and soil quality, pesticide use and waste recycling and reduction. Our departments are at the forefront of environmental science, using the most recent research to shape the state’s environmental laws. The Office of the Secretary heads CalEPA overseeing and coordinating the activities of one office, two boards, and three departments dedicated to improving California’s environment.

title:
Why many U.S. community water systems struggle to support large industrial-scale loads?

I saw a US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) study on community water systems in the United States. Link:‚Ä¶ | Shaolei Ren
description:
Why many U.S. community water systems struggle to support large industrial-scale loads?

I saw a US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) study on community water systems in the United States. Link: https://lnkd.in/gtzuCu8g

The numbers are interesting.

About 90% of community water systems serve fewer than 10,000 people, and their median surplus physical capacity is only about 0.2 million gallons per day (MGD). The remaining 10% of systems serve more than 10,000 people, and their median surplus capacity is about 3 MGD. (See comments for technical rigor.)

Three important caveats:

 üîπ The "surplus capacity" numbers are based on physical design limits.
In practice, utilities maintain safety margins for extended heat waves, droughts, and fire suppression. In addition, capacity that has already been allocated to existing users is often much higher than their current usage. As a result, the actual capacity available for new users is typically much smaller than the design surplus suggests.

üîπ Treatment capacity is only one piece of the system.

The EPA numbers refer primarily to treatment plant capacity. In reality, other components can become bottlenecks: distribution pipes, storage tanks, pumps
wastewater treatment systems (although technically not part of community water systems). These constraints often limit how much additional demand a system can accommodate.

üîπ The data is old.
 The EPA data referenced above was published in 2011 based on a 2006 survey. Nearly two decades have passed. Has the situation improved significantly? It is not obvious. A more recent EPA report to Congress estimates that U.S. drinking water and wastewater infrastructure faces about $1.3 trillion in funding needs over the next 20 years, suggesting that infrastructure challenges may have worsened rather than improved.

Now consider the scale of new large industrial water demand.

Some recent projects require several million gallons per day, for example:
üîπ ~8 MGD (scheduled for delivery in 2031) in a town in Indiana
üîπ 2-8 MGD in a town in Virginia

In the Virginia case, the community's previous plan to identify new water sources around 2060 now need to accelerate to the present, because developing new sources can take many years and is constrained by hydrology, regulation, and environmental limits.

Could utilities simply remove existing users to make room for new ones?

In practice, that is difficult due to water rights allocations, contracts, and legal constraints.

The logic is intuitive: When we walk into a restaurant, we only sit at an empty table. Similarly, when utilities connect a large new user, they only allocate what capacity is truly available.

This helps explain why many communities in the U.S. struggle to support new industrial-scale water demand today.

But constraints also drive innovation. Just as we are innovating in the power system to accommodate new loads, the water sector may soon face a similar wave of innovation.

title: The economics of elusive methane diplomacy: forecasting 2030 emissions in China, India, and Russia - Humanities and Social Sciences Communications
description: Reduction of anthropogenic methane emissions poses a substantial imperative in the context of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius. However, due to the detrimental effects of methane reduction policies on economic growth, public finance, social stability, vulnerable rural communities and employment, countries do not show strong political will on this issue, producing negative externalities on a global scale. To tackle this, 160 countries, which account for 59% of the emissions, signed the Global Methane Pledge, promising to reduce their emissions by 30% by 2030 relative to their 2020 levels. However, China, India, and Russia—the first, third, and fourth largest emitters, respectively—did not join the commitment. This paper aims to estimate methane emissions for these countries and elucidate the economic factors impeding their mitigation. Using annual data from Climate Watch (1990-2022), we apply two univariate machine learning forecasting methods—Autometrics and XGBoost—to project emissions through 2030. Our baseline projections reveal that methane emissions for all three countries will continue to increase, totaling 2896 MtCO2e in 2030. Our 2030 estimates indicate that, collectively, methane emissions from these three countries will be 7.04% above 2020 levels. Fossil fuel trade relationships between these countries, low labor productivity, and social costs related to energy and employment are the main explanatory factors. Our findings highlight the significant gap between global commitments and the economic realities of the major emitters. Policy implications state the urgency of prioritizing energy-sector methane abatement as the least costly way of combatting global warming and advancing methane diplomacy to facilitate equitable technology transfer and coordination strategies.
